newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Munich Re sees profit surge slowing.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Munich Re sees profit surge slowing.

text.p: Munich Re, the world's leading reinsurance group, on Monday gave a modest outlook for its current year earnings after profits surged by more than 80 percent in the 1995-1996 period.
Management board chairman Hans-Juergen Schinzler said costs associated with the group's multi-billion dollar takeover of American Re would likely weigh on earnings this year.
Its record earnings per share of 140 marks achieved in 1995-1996 were unlikely to be repeated, he said.

"We had an unusually high jump in earnings this year and this does not go on into infinity. It can be that we will take a breather this year, but at a very high level," Schinzler told a news conference.

The reinsurer, fully called Muenchener Rueckversicherungs AG, reported 1995-1996 net profit of 595 million marks ($395.8 million) as group underwriting earnings leaped to 573 million marks from a 100-million-mark loss in the year-ago period.

Munich Re had already announced plans to raise its dividend for the year to 16 marks from 13.50 marks. Schinzler said there was a "50-50" chance that the payout could be raised in the current year, depending on how earnings develop.
"We really wanted to get the dividend to a level that could also be sustained through bad times," he said.

While the Munich Re parent company was likely to maintain its current underwriting earnings in 1996-1997, Schinzler said the group's global reinsurance units would be unlikely to match their performance of the past year.
Schinzler said he hoped the acquisition of American Re, which ranks third in the U.S. reinsurance market, could be completed by the end of November, once approval from authorities had been secured.
But Munich Re will not consolidate American Re in its accounts until 1997-1998, by which time the group will be able to "reap the full benefits" of its investment, Schinzler said.

American Re, which is to merge with Munich Re's Munich American Reinsurance Company but retain its name, posted earnings of $97.5 million in the first six months of 1996 and should post good earnings for the full year, Schinzler said.
"We considered it desirable for a long time to expand our inadequate position in the biggest insurance market in the world (the U.S.). Now we have done so," he said.

Munich Re said in August that it would spend $3.3 billion on American Re, its second major acquisition in a year. It also plans a takeover of health insurer Deutsche Krankenversicherungs AG (DKV) in a share swap with Allianz AG.
Schinzler said the DKV acquisition formed part of Munich Re's strategy to boost its market share in retail insurance.

DKV will be consolidated into group accounts in the current year, adding some four billion marks to Munich Re's group direct insurance premium income and bringing a "positive impact" on group earnings.

As to future possible acquisitions in France where Munich Re lags well behind rivals SCOR and Swiss Re, Schinzler said the group saw no potential takeover targets but was still keen to improve its market share in the region.
It was unlikely that Munich Re would seek a capital increase this year after already raising its capital in 1995.

The group also has no plans to sell its 25 percent stake in fellow insurance giant Allianz AG Holding, which Schinzler said would yield about 15 billion marks, but the sum would be cut by more than half by tax charges.
Allianz and Munich Re, longtime close partners with major cross shareholdings, would remain so, Schinzler said.
Munich Re's shares closed 65 marks lower at 3,730 in DAX floor trading. In late electronic trade, its shares stood at 3,748 marks each, 37 down on the day.
The group had already released most of its earnings data, including the market-moving earnings per share figure. ($1=1.5033 Mark)
